authority: Only the supplied seed exercise prose and concept blocks 0, 7, 9, 12. No answers, interactions, previous choices, diagrams, solved examples, or other ticket outputs were consulted.

definitions.sphere: Concept 0: all points M satisfying |SM|=R, with R>0.
definitions.ball: Concept 7: all points M satisfying |SM|<=R, with R>0.
definitions.origin_equation: Concept 12: x^2+y^2+z^2=R^2 when the center is O.

tasks: Prove that the center is a symmetry center of the ball.
Determine how many symmetry axes and symmetry planes a sphere has.
conditions: R>0 follows from the selected definitions.
Part 1 uses the source word for the ball; the same central reflection also preserves its boundary sphere.
An axis is an entire line and a symmetry plane is an entire plane.
derivation: Let the central reflection be T(M)=2S-M. Then T(M)-S=S-M, so |ST(M)|=|SM| for every M.
For every M in the ball, |SM|<=R implies |ST(M)|<=R; T(T(M))=M proves this is a bijection of the whole ball onto itself, not merely a one-way inclusion. Equality |SM|=R is preserved as well.
For any line through S, a half-turn about that line fixes S and preserves distances. More generally every rotation about that line does so. Thus every line through S is a symmetry axis of the sphere.
For any plane through S, reflection in that plane fixes S and preserves distances, so every plane through S is a symmetry plane.
There are infinitely many distinct line directions and infinitely many distinct planes through S. Hence the sphere has infinitely many symmetry axes and infinitely many symmetry planes.

These are precisely the axes and planes through S: a sphere has a unique center, so an isometry preserving the sphere must fix S. To see uniqueness, if S+w were another center of radius R, then for every unit vector u the two boundary points S+Ru and S-Ru would give |Ru-w|^2=|-Ru-w|^2, hence u dot w=0 for every u and w=0. A half-turn fixes exactly its axis; a plane reflection fixes exactly its plane.
solutions.result: The center is a symmetry center of the ball and its boundary sphere; the sphere has infinitely many symmetry axes and infinitely many symmetry planes, exactly all lines and planes through S.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: A distance-preserving, self-inverse map establishes set invariance; counting coordinate axes or coordinate planes is not counting all symmetry axes or planes.
solutions.choice_capacity_risk: Recognizing a decisive invariant and correct symmetry families cannot demonstrate independently constructing the original central-symmetry proof.

tasks: Identify the intersection of a sphere with a plane through its center.
conditions: The object is the sphere, not the filled ball.
The plane contains the center S and R>0.
derivation: Choose perpendicular unit vectors e1,e2 in the plane. Every point of the plane is M=S+u e1+v e2.
|SM|^2=u^2+v^2. Membership in the sphere requires equality u^2+v^2=R^2.
This planar locus is the circumference of a circle centered at S of radius R, a great circle. The center S itself is not in the intersection because |SS|=0<R.
solutions.result: A circle circumference centered at S with radius R, not a filled disk.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: Equality gives the circle boundary; the ball's inequality would instead give a disk.
solutions.choice_capacity_risk: Selecting a locus description does not demonstrate independently writing a sectional-locus justification.

tasks: Determine every listed point belonging to the sphere centered at S(1,-2,0) with radius 3.
conditions: Sphere membership requires squared distance exactly 9, not at most 9.
derivation: A-S=(0,0,3), so |SA|^2=0+0+9=9: A is on the sphere.
B-S=(2,-1,1), so |SB|^2=4+1+1=6: B is inside the sphere, not on it.
C-S=(0,3,sqrt(2)), so |SC|^2=0+9+2=11: C is outside the sphere.
D-S=(-1,-1,sqrt(7)), so |SD|^2=1+1+7=9: D is on the sphere.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: Apply the same center-relative, exact-distance predicate to every candidate, including radical coordinates and an interior point.
solutions.choice_capacity_risk: Selecting all qualifying points retains the classification but does not require a written four-point distance calculation.

tasks: Find all intersections of x^2+y^2+z^2=R^2 with the three coordinate axes.
conditions: R>0 is the radius convention supplied by concept 0.
Each coordinate axis is a whole line, including both signs.
derivation: On the x-axis y=z=0, hence x^2=R^2 and x=R or x=-R.
On the y-axis x=z=0, hence y=R or y=-R.
On the z-axis x=y=0, hence z=R or z=-R.
Since R>0, these are six distinct points and no other axis points satisfy the equation.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: Solving a square equation on a whole axis yields both signs; R^2 is not the coordinate magnitude.
solutions.choice_capacity_risk: Recognizing the complete coordinate set does not demonstrate independently producing that set.

tasks: Find every intersection of the sphere x^2+y^2+z^2=200 with the line SO for S(3,4,5) and O the origin.
conditions: SO is the full line, not a ray or segment.
The center of this sphere is O; S is only a point determining the line.
derivation: Parametrize the entire line as M(t)=(3t,4t,5t) with t any real number.
Substitution gives (9+16+25)t^2=200, so 50t^2=200, t^2=4, and t=2 or t=-2.
Therefore M(2)=(6,8,10) and M(-2)=(-6,-8,-10). Both have squared norm 36+64+100=200 and lie on SO.
|OS|^2=50<200, so S itself is an interior point rather than an intersection.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: A scalar parametrization preserves the line direction and both real roots; line intersections differ from ray or segment intersections.
solutions.choice_capacity_risk: Selecting a complete intersection pair does not demonstrate independently deriving the line parametrization and solving it.

tasks: Find the distance from A(3p,-2p,6p) to the sphere x^2+y^2+z^2=p^2.
conditions: p>0 is explicit in the source.
Distance to a set means the minimum Euclidean distance to a point on that set.
derivation: |OA|=sqrt((9+4+36)p^2)=sqrt(49p^2)=7p, using p>0. The sphere has radius p, so A is outside it.
For any point M on the sphere, the reverse triangle inequality gives |AM|>=||OA|-|OM||=7p-p=6p.
Take M=A/7=(3p/7,-2p/7,6p/7). Its squared norm is p^2 and it lies on the segment OA.
|A-M|=(6/7)|OA|=6p, so the lower bound is attained and is the requested distance.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: The minimum distance subtracts the radius from the center distance for this exterior point; it is not the farthest distance or a difference of squared norms.
solutions.choice_capacity_risk: Selecting a distance does not demonstrate independently establishing the lower bound and its attainment.

tasks: Write the sphere equation for center S(2,-1,3), radius 4.
Write the sphere equation for center S(-5,0,7), radius sqrt(3).
conditions: The two center-radius specifications are separate requested spheres.
Use coordinate-minus-center signs and the squared radius on the right-hand side.
These are sphere equalities, not ball inequalities.
derivation: From |SM|=R, square the distance formula to obtain (x-a)^2+(y-b)^2+(z-c)^2=R^2.
Expanding the first equation gives x^2+y^2+z^2-4x+2y-6z-2=0, because 4+1+9-16=-2.
Expanding the second equation gives x^2+y^2+z^2+10x-14z+71=0, because 25+49-3=71.
solutions.conceptual_distinction: Negative center coordinates change the subtraction sign; a radius and its square are different quantities, including a radical radius.
solutions.choice_capacity_risk: Recognizing a coherent equation pair cannot demonstrate independently constructing each equation from the distance formula.
